summary: ML-KEM is a quantum-resistant key encapsulation mechanism. This document specifies conventions for using it in X.509 PKI, including subject public keys and private keys.

eli5.summary: ML-KEM lets two parties agree on a secret key in a way even quantum computers should not crack. This explains how certificates hold such keys.

questions: how are ml-kem keys stored in x509 certificates
what is the ml-kem private key seed format
subtitle: How to put quantum-resistant ML-KEM keys into X.509 certificates and private key files.

tldr.problem: ML-KEM is a quantum-resistant way to agree on a shared secret, but X.509 certificates had no agreed identifiers or encodings for its keys.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns each of the three ML-KEM parameter sets an NIST object identifier, defines how the public key sits in a certificate with no algorithm parameters, limits key usage to keyEncipherment, and defines three private key encodings built around a 64-byte seed.
tldr.outcome: Certificate authorities and software can now carry ML-KEM keys in standard PKIX certificates, and the seed-only private key format is the recommended one. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9935 is a Standards Track Proposed Standard published in March 2026, and it is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC. RFC 9936 uses these certificate conventions for ML-KEM in the Cryptographic Message Syntax.

sections.title: What the RFC Covers
sections.content:
The Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM) is a quantum-resistant Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) standardized by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in FIPS 203. Before standardization, versions of it were known as Kyber, and ML-KEM and Kyber are not compatible.

This document specifies how to use ML-KEM in Public Key Infrastructure using X.509 (PKIX) certificates at three security levels: ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024. It uses object identifiers (OIDs) assigned by NIST and also specifies the private key format.

ML-KEM certificates are meant for protocols where the public key is used to generate and encapsulate a shared secret, from which a symmetric key is derived to encrypt a payload; RFC 9936 is the CMS example. For TLS, the RFC says such certificates could only be end-entity identity certificates and would need significant protocol updates.
sections.eli5: ML-KEM is a lock that is meant to stay safe even against future super-computers. This RFC says how to describe that lock on an ID card and how to store its key.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content:
A certificate names its algorithm with an AlgorithmIdentifier: an algorithm field holding an OID and an optional parameters field. For an ML-KEM public key the algorithm MUST be one of the NIST id-alg-ml-kem OIDs, chosen by security level, and the parameters field MUST be absent.

The three OIDs sit under the NIST kems arc: id-alg-ml-kem-512 is { kems 1 }, id-alg-ml-kem-768 is { kems 2 } and id-alg-ml-kem-1024 is { kems 3 }.
sections.eli5: Each size of the lock has its own name tag, like a model number. The tag alone says which one it is, so nothing else needs to be written next to it.

sections.title: Subject Public Key Fields
sections.content:
In a certificate, the subjectPublicKeyInfo field holds an algorithm identifier and a subjectPublicKey, the byte stream of the public key. For ML-KEM the key has no ASN.1 wrapping inside that field, and its size is fixed by the parameter set: 800 octets for ML-KEM-512, 1184 for ML-KEM-768 and 1568 for ML-KEM-1024.

When a public key appears outside a SubjectPublicKeyInfo in an ASN.1 environment, it can be encoded as an OCTET STRING of the matching size. Private keys are covered by the format in the Private Key Format section.
sections.eli5: The public key goes into the ID card as a plain block of bytes. The size is fixed for each lock model, like each key blank having one standard length.

sections.title: Key Usage Bits
sections.content:
The keyUsage certificate extension says what a key is meant for. If the extension is present in a certificate whose SubjectPublicKeyInfo uses an id-alg-ml-kem-* OID, then keyEncipherment MUST be the only key usage set.

In other words, an ML-KEM certificate is not allowed to double as a signing certificate.
sections.eli5: The ID card says what the key may be used for. An ML-KEM key may only be used for locking up secret keys and nothing else.

sections.title: Private Key Format
sections.content:
FIPS 203 defines two private key forms: a 64-octet seed and the expanded private key, called the decapsulation key. The seed is split into two 32-octet halves, d and z, and expanded with ML-KEM.KeyGen_internal(d,z). A key pair is made by drawing 64 random octets from a cryptographically secure random number generator.

The private key is carried in the privateKey field of an OneAsymmetricKey (from RFC 5958) as a CHOICE of three forms:

  • seed: just the 64-byte seed, tagged [0].
  • expandedKey: only the expanded private key, 1632, 2400 or 3168 octets for ML-KEM-512, 768 and 1024.
  • both: a sequence with the seed and the expanded key, so that software that keeps only one form can still interoperate.

The seed-only form is RECOMMENDED because it is the most compact and both the expanded key and the public key can be derived from it. Parsers should tell the forms apart by their ASN.1 tag (0x80 for seed, 0x04 for expandedKey, 0x30 for both) and not by guessing from length.
sections.eli5: You can keep either a short recipe card (the seed) or the whole finished cake (the expanded key), or both. The recipe card is smaller and can always remake the cake, so it is the one the RFC prefers.

sections.title: Implementation and Consistency Checks
sections.content:
FIPS 203's main key generation routine does not hand the seed back to the caller, and the seed-expansion routine is labelled internal. The RFC suggests a variant that also returns the seed, and says the seed-expansion algorithm should be promoted to a main algorithm for external use.

Expanding a seed is a one-way step: once the seed is thrown away it cannot be recovered from the expanded key. So implementations are RECOMMENDED to keep and export the seed, even when they also export the expanded key.

When a private key arrives in the both form, the recipient SHOULD run a seed consistency check: regenerate the expanded form from the seed and confirm it is bytewise equal to the expanded key received. If the two do not match, the recipient MUST reject the key as malformed. For a received expandedKey, FIPS 203 requires a hash check before use.
sections.eli5: Once you throw away the recipe card you cannot get it back from the cake. So keep the card. If someone gives you both, bake from the card and see if it matches their cake.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5280 apply. Protecting the private key material (the seed) is vital, because disclosure can lead to masquerades. Key generation relies on random numbers, and a weak random number generator can leave an attacker a small set of possibilities to search; FIPS 203 has specific randomness requirements.

The private key format also affects binding properties that some protocols need beyond basic IND-CCA security. Citing published analysis, the RFC says ML-KEM with the expanded key format is not MAL-BIND-K-CT or MAL-BIND-K-PK secure, and that the 64-byte seed format adds MAL-BIND-K-CT security but still not MAL-BIND-K-PK.
sections.eli5: Keep the key secret and make it with truly random dice. How you store the key can also change some extra kinds of safety, and the short seed form is a bit safer.

items.title: seed
items.text: 64 bytes, tag [0]. Recommended; everything else can be derived.

items.title: expandedKey
items.text: Only the expanded decapsulation key. The seed cannot be recovered from it.

items.title: both
items.text: Seed and expanded key together, so receivers can run a consistency check.
